claim: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus pseudintermedius (MRSP) is an important emerging zoonotic pathogen that causes severe skin infections.
source: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus pseudintermedius (MRSP) is an important emerging zoonotic pathogen that causes severe skin infections.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about MRSP as a pathogen.

claim: A unique strain (S. felis C4) was isolated from feline skin that inhibited MRSP and multiple gram-positive pathogens.
source: A unique strain (S. felis C4) was isolated from feline skin that inhibited MRSP and multiple gram-positive pathogens.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the screening and antimicrobial assays described in the manuscript.

claim: Whole genome sequencing and mass spectrometry revealed several secreted antimicrobials including a thiopeptide bacteriocin micrococcin P1 and phenol-soluble modulin beta (PSMβ) peptides.
source: Whole genome sequencing and mass spectrometry revealed several secreted antimicrobials including a thiopeptide bacteriocin micrococcin P1 and phenol-soluble modulin beta (PSMβ) peptides that exhibited antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole genome sequencing and mass spectrometry analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: PSMβ peptides exhibited antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity.
source: Whole genome sequencing and mass spectrometry revealed several secreted antimicrobials including a thiopeptide bacteriocin micrococcin P1 and phenol-soluble modulin beta (PSMβ) peptides that exhibited antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from antimicrobial assays and inflammatory response studies.

claim: S. felis antimicrobials inhibited translation and disrupted bacterial but not eukaryotic cell membranes.
source: Fluorescence and electron microscopy revealed that S. felis antimicrobials inhibited translation and disrupted bacterial but not eukaryotic cell membranes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fluorescence microscopy, electron microscopy, and cytotoxicity assays.

claim: S. felis significantly reduced MRSP skin colonization in competition experiments in mice.
source: Competition experiments in mice showed that S. felis significantly reduced MRSP skin colonization and an antimicrobial extract from S. felis significantly reduced necrotic skin injury from MRSP infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo mouse colonization experiments.

claim: An antimicrobial extract from S. felis significantly reduced necrotic skin injury from MRSP infection in mice.
source: Competition experiments in mice showed that S. felis significantly reduced MRSP skin colonization and an antimicrobial extract from S. felis significantly reduced necrotic skin injury from MRSP infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo mouse infection experiments.

claim: Skin is colonized by hundreds of diverse bacterial species that exist within a complex and dynamic chemical landscape.
source: Skin is colonized by hundreds of diverse bacterial species that exist within a complex and dynamic chemical landscape.
evidence: This is a statement that draws from established scientific knowledge about the skin microbiome.

claim: Chemical interactions on skin can play important roles in skin health, immune education and protection against pathogen colonization and infection.
source: These chemical interactions can play important roles in skin health, immune education and protection against pathogen colonization and infection (Sanford and Gallo, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The composition of the skin microbial community of humans and animals varies extensively, in part due to different skin habitats.
source: The composition of the skin microbial community of humans and animals varies extensively, in part due to different skin habitats, that is increased hair density in animals, as well as more subtle differences in the chemical and biological conditions of the skin (Grice and Segre, 2011; Ross et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The human microbial skin community is distinct from and significantly less diverse than that of both wild and domestic animals.
source: Overall, the human microbial skin community is distinct from and significantly less diverse than that of both wild and domestic animals (Ross et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Human skin is generally dominated by few taxa present at high abundance for example cutibacteria, streptococci, and staphylococci.
source: Human skin is generally dominated by few taxa present at high abundance for example cutibacteria, streptococci, and staphylococci, whereas canine skin harbors a more equally distributed and diverse group of taxa (Song et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Canine skin harbors a more equally distributed and diverse group of taxa compared to human skin.
source: Human skin is generally dominated by few taxa present at high abundance for example cutibacteria, streptococci, and staphylococci, whereas canine skin harbors a more equally distributed and diverse group of taxa (Song et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Close contact between humans and animals can be a source for microbial transmission.
source: Naturally, close contact between humans and animals can be a source for microbial transmission (Frana et al., 2013; Lai et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Exposure to pets early in life can be protective against atopic disease in later life.
source: Although it remains to be determined if shared taxa are stable over time, there are reports that exposure to pets early in life can be protective against atopic disease in later life (Mandhane et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: There are many documented cases of human staphylococcal infection from epidemiological exposure to dogs.
source: In contrast, there are also many documented cases of human staphylococcal infection from epidemiological exposure to dogs (Somayaji et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Companion animals can act as reservoirs for methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) and more commonly, S. pseudintermedius (MRSP).
source: Companion animals can act as reservoirs for methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) and more commonly, S. pseudintermedius (MRSP), with both species sharing many common invasion and virulence factors (Garbacz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: S. aureus and S. pseudintermedius share many common invasion and virulence factors.
source: Companion animals can act as reservoirs for methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA) and more commonly, S. pseudintermedius (MRSP), with both species sharing many common invasion and virulence factors (Garbacz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The zoonotic significance of S. pseudintermedius may have been previously underestimated because it was frequently misidentified as S. aureus in human wound infections.
source: The zoonotic significance of S. pseudintermedius may have been previously underestimated because it was frequently misidentified as S. aureus in human wound infections (Börjesson et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: More advanced diagnostic techniques such as MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry have led to increased detection of human S. pseudintermedius infections.
source: More advanced diagnostic techniques such as matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization-time of flight (MALDI-TOF) mass spectrometry have led to increased detection of human S. pseudintermedius infections (Ference et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Colonization of S. pseudintermedius is a contributing factor in canine atopic dermatitis (AD).
source: Colonization of S. pseudintermedius is a contributing factor in canine atopic dermatitis (AD).
evidence: This is a statement that draws from established scientific knowledge.

claim: The prevalence of AD in humans and AD in dogs are similar (10–15% in US).
source: Interestingly, the prevalence of AD in humans and AD in dogs are similar (10–15% in US) and present with remarkably similar immunological and clinical manifestations (Marsella and Girolomoni, 2009; Silverberg, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: AD in humans and dogs present with remarkably similar immunological and clinical manifestations.
source: Interestingly, the prevalence of AD in humans and AD in dogs are similar (10–15% in US) and present with remarkably similar immunological and clinical manifestations (Marsella and Girolomoni, 2009; Silverberg, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Several studies have reported a decrease in the microbiome diversity of AD and increased colonization of S aureus in humans and S. pseudintermedius in dogs.
source: Likewise, several studies have reported a decrease in the microbiome diversity of AD and increased colonization of S aureus in humans and S. pseudintermedius in dogs (Fazakerley et al., 2009; Nakatsuji and Gallo, 2019; Older et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: In human AD, S. aureus was identified in higher relative abundances during disease flares.
source: In human AD, S. aureus was identified in higher relative abundances during disease flares (Kong et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The relative abundance of S. pseudintermedius was shown to increase with disease flares in canine AD.
source: Similarly, the relative abundance of S. pseudintermedius was also shown to increase with disease flares in canine AD (Bradley et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Dilute bleach baths are a common antiseptic treatment for AD, with the goal of reducing the carriage of staphylococci.
source: Dilute bleach baths are a common antiseptic treatment for AD, with the goal of reducing the carriage of staphylococci (Banovic et al., 2018; Chopra et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The effectiveness of bleach baths as an antibacterial agent is controversial.
source: However, its effectiveness as an antibacterial agent is controversial (Sawada et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Commensal staphylococcus strains that produce lantibiotics reduced S. aureus counts and improved clinical outcome when applied to skin of patients with AD.
source: A recent successful example of this approach is the discovery and use of commensal staphylococcus strains that produce lantibiotics that when applied to skin of patients with AD reduced S. aureus counts and improved clinical outcome (Nakatsuji et al., 2021a; Nakatsuji et al., 2021b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Other studies have identified antimicrobial activity in some staphylococcus strains belonging to species of S. lugdunensis, S. epidermidis, and S. capitis.
source: Other studies have also identified antimicrobial activity in some staphylococcus strains belonging to species of S. lugdunensis (Zipperer et al., 2016), S. epidermidis (Cogen et al., 2010), and S. capitis (O'Neill et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Very little is known regarding the antimicrobial activity of staphylococci derived from the animal commensal microbiome and their clinical potential against skin infection.
source: In contrast, very little is known regarding the antimicrobial activity of staphylococci derived from the animal commensal microbiome and their clinical potential against skin infection.
evidence: This is a statement that draws from established scientific knowledge and identifies a gap in the literature.

claim: S. felis C4 produced a thiopeptide bacteriocin and several α-helical amphipathic peptides with antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity.
source: S. felis C4 produced a thiopeptide bacteriocin and several α-helical amphipathic peptides with antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry, antimicrobial assays, and inflammatory response studies.

claim: Fifty-eight staphylococcus isolates across the coagulase-positive (CoPS) and coagulase-negative (CoNS) groups were screened for antimicrobial activity against MRSP ST71.
source: Fifty-eight staphylococcus isolates across the coagulase-positive (CoPS) and coagulase-negative (CoNS) groups were screened, including validated antimicrobial strains of human origin, S. hominis A9 (Nakatsuji et al., 2017) and S. capitis E12 (O'Neill et al., 2020) and a non-active S. aureus 113 negative control strain (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the screening assay and is illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Five strains demonstrated greater than 80% inhibition of S. pseudintermedius growth across all three different dilutions of supernatant (1:1, 1:4, 1:8).
source: Amongst all test isolates, five strains demonstrated greater than 80 % inhibition of S. pseudintermedius growth (dashed line) across all three different dilutions of supernatant (1:1, 1:4, 1:8) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the antimicrobial screening assay shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The five positive hit strains exhibited greater potency compared to the positive control S. hominis A9 supernatant.
source: Surprisingly, these strains exhibited greater potency compared to the positive control S. hominis A9 supernatant (indicated by black circle), which inhibited growth of S. pseudintermedius in a 1:1 dilution, but not at 1:4 or lower.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing the antimicrobial activity of different strains.

claim: Amongst the five positive hits, three were identified as S. felis and two S. pseudintermedius.
source: Amongst the five positive hits, three were identified as S. felis and two S. pseudintermedius.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the screening and species identification.

claim: All five isolates including positive control S. hominis A9 produced an observable zone of inhibition against S. pseudintermedius during live co-culture on agar.
source: In the second independent antimicrobial assay, all five isolates including positive control S. hominis A9, produced an observable zone of inhibition against S. pseudintermedius during live co-culture on agar (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the agar co-culture assay shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The two feline S. felis species (C4, N26) produced the largest inhibitory zones, extending 3.0–3.3 mm outward from the edge of the growing colony.
source: The two feline S. felis species (C4, N26 labelled with white arrows) produced the largest inhibitory zones, extending 3.0–3.3 mm outward from the edge of the growing colony.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the agar co-culture assay with measurements of inhibition zones.

claim: Of the four gram-negative strains tested, only moderate inhibition was demonstrated after 18 hr incubation with 80–100% of the S. felis C4 supernatant.
source: Of the four gram-negative strains tested, only moderate inhibition was demonstrated after 18 hr incubation with 80–100% of the S. felis C4 supernatant (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from antimicrobial assays shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Bacterial culture in the presence of just 1–5% of S. felis C4 supernatant was sufficient to inhibit >80% growth of all four gram-positive organisms, including S. pseudintermedius, E. faecium, B. subtilis, and S. aureus.
source: In contrast, bacterial culture in the presence of just 1–5% of S. felis C4 supernatant was sufficient to inhibit >80% growth of all four gram-positive organisms, including S. pseudintermedius, E. faecium, B. subtilis, and S. aureus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from antimicrobial assays.

claim: Of the three antimicrobial S. felis isolates, only the C4 supernatant retained activity after precipitation with 75% ammonium sulfate (AS).
source: Of the three antimicrobial S. felis isolates, only the C4 supernatant retained activity after precipitation with 75 % ammonium sulfate (AS) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from precipitation and antimicrobial assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 75% AS was highly effective in precipitating the antimicrobial factor(s) from the C4 supernatant since no activity could be visualized in the non-precipitate fraction.
source: Moreover, 75 % AS was highly effective in precipitating the antimicrobial factor(s) from the C4 supernatant since no activity could be visualized in the non-precipitate fraction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from precipitation and antimicrobial assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The antimicrobial effect was also achieved with a simpler extraction by n-butanol.
source: This effect was also achieved with a simpler extraction by n-butanol.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from extraction and antimicrobial assays.

claim: The antimicrobial butanol extract remained active up to 1 week at room temperature (RT) and was stable after boiling.
source: The antimicrobial butanol extract remained active up to 1 week at room temperature (RT) and was stable after boiling (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from stability testing shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The butanol extraction provided a partially purified and enriched antimicrobial fraction compared to that of the crude supernatant and AS precipitation.
source: As expected, the butanol extraction provided a partially purified and enriched antimicrobial fraction compared to that of the crude supernatant and AS precipitation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from protein analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The S. felis extract was found to be effective against multiple clinical isolates of S. aureus and S. pseudintermedius with a MIC range of 0.4–6.25 μg/ml.
source: The S. felis extract was found to be effective against multiple clinical isolates of S. aureus and S. pseudintermedius with a MIC range of 0.4–6.25 μg/ml (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from MIC assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Some CoNS strains, including S. hominis and S. lugdunensis were less sensitive and had a higher MIC of 12.5 μg/ml.
source: In contrast, some CoNS strains, including S. hominis and S. lugdunensis were less sensitive and had a higher MIC of 12.5 μg/ml.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from MIC assays.

claim: Most clinically-derived S. pseudintermedius strains are biofilm producers.
source: Reports have shown that most clinically-derived S. pseudintermedius strains are biofilm producers (Singh et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: A 4 hr preformed biofilm of pseudintermedius ST71 showed a significant decrease in crystal violet (CV) staining over time when incubated with 100% conditioned supernatant of S. felis C4.
source: A 4 hr preformed biofilm of pseudintermedius ST71 showed a significant decrease in crystal violet (CV) staining over time, when incubated with 100 % conditioned supernatant of S. felis C4, indicating biofilm disruption and degradation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from biofilm assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The S. felis C4 extract had anti-biofilm activity similar to crude conditioned supernatant, with biofilm mass reduced by 48% at 250 μg/ml and 58% at 500 μg/ml.
source: The S. felis C4 extract had anti-biofilm activity similar to crude conditioned supernatant, with biofilm mass reduced by 48 % at 250 μg/ml and 58 % at 500 μg/ml (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from biofilm assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: HPLC purification of sterile culture supernatant yielded two major peaks that eluted at 44% and 47% acetonitrile.
source: To determine the nature of the antimicrobial product produced by S. felis C4, sterile culture supernatant was purified by HPLC. This yielded two major peaks that eluted at 44% and 47% acetonitrile (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from HPLC purification shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Anti-S. pseudintermedius activity was predominantly associated with fraction 32 which eluted at 47% acetonitrile.
source: Anti-S. pseudintermedius activity was predominantly associated with fraction 32 which eluted at 47 % acetonitrile (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from HPLC purification and antimicrobial assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SDS PAGE and protein silver staining of the active and inactive fractions revealed a unique band of roughly 5 kDa in size in the active fraction 32.
source: SDS PAGE and protein silver staining of the active and inactive fractions revealed a unique band of roughly 5 kDa in size in the active fraction 32 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from SDS PAGE and silver staining shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Only the ≤5 kDa band demonstrated antimicrobial activity after incubation with S. pseudintermedius.
source: To determine if this small protein was responsible for antimicrobial activity, gel slices of the fraction 32 lane corresponding to small, medium and larger proteins ( ≤ 5 kDa, 5–20 kDa and 20–50 kDa, respectively) were excised and extracted by acetone precipitation as previously described (Botelho et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2015). Only the ≤5 kDa band demonstrated antimicrobial activity after incubation with S. pseudintermedius (Figure 2D), thereby suggesting the likely candidate to be a small peptide.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from gel extraction and antimicrobial assays shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mass spectrometry (MS) analysis of the top eight hits in the active and non-active HPLC fractions identified several putative small antimicrobial peptides (AMP), representing the phenol soluble modulin beta (PSMβ1–3) and gamma (PSMγ, aka delta-hemolysin) families and a peptide of unknown function containing the EF-HAND domain.
source: Mass spectrometry (MS) analysis of the top eight hits in the active and non-active HPLC fractions identified several putative small antimicrobial peptides (AMP), representing the phenol soluble modulin beta (PSMβ1–3) and gamma (PSMγ, aka delta-hemolysin) families and a peptide of unknown function containing the EF-HAND domain, common amongst some antimicrobial Ca2+ binding proteins, such as S100A8/S100A9 (Chazin, 2011; Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Whole genome analysis of the S. felis C4 strain confirmed the presence of three PSMβ-encoding genes.
source: Whole genome analysis of the S. felis C4 strain confirmed the presence of three PSMβ-encoding genes (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from whole genome sequencing shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Based on sequence similarities to mammalian cationic AMPs such as cathelicidin LL-37 the PSMβ and EF-HAND domain peptides were predicted to have α-helical amphipathic structure.
source: Based on sequence similarities to mammalian cationic AMPs such as cathelicidin LL-37 the PSMβ and EF-HAND domain peptides were predicted to have α-helical amphipathic structure (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from sequence analysis and structural predictions shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The positive control cytotoxic PSMγ induced maximal cell death with 100% LDH release at 62.5 ug/ml.
source: The positive control cytotoxic PSMγ induced maximal cell death with 100 % LDH release at 62.5 ug/ml, yet at this concentration none of the PSMβ peptides nor the crude S. felis extract exceeded 20 % LDH release (Figure 2H), suggesting that S. felis C4 PSMβs are not cytotoxic.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cytotoxicity assays shown in Figure 2H.

claim: At 62.5 ug/ml, none of the PSMβ peptides nor the crude S. felis extract exceeded 20% LDH release.
source: The positive control cytotoxic PSMγ induced maximal cell death with 100 % LDH release at 62.5 ug/ml, yet at this concentration none of the PSMβ peptides nor the crude S. felis extract exceeded 20 % LDH release (Figure 2H), suggesting that S. felis C4 PSMβs are not cytotoxic.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cytotoxicity assays shown in Figure 2H.

claim: S. felis C4 PSMβs are not cytotoxic.
source: The positive control cytotoxic PSMγ induced maximal cell death with 100 % LDH release at 62.5 ug/ml, yet at this concentration none of the PSMβ peptides nor the crude S. felis extract exceeded 20 % LDH release (Figure 2H), suggesting that S. felis C4 PSMβs are not cytotoxic.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data from cytotoxicity assays shown in Figure 2H.

claim: A defined role for PSMβ in mediating host interactions has been largely unexplored.
source: Unlike the well-characterized cytolytic and inflammatory activities of PSMα, a defined role for PSMβ in mediating host interactions has been largely unexplored (Da et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Neither PSMβ nor the extract resulted in any detectable increase in gene expression in NHEKs.
source: Neither PSMβ nor the extract resulted in any detectable increase in gene expression, whereas MALP-2 significantly increased the expression of hBD-2, and Poly I:C significantly increased CXCL10 and IL-6 expression (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qPCR shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: MALP-2 significantly increased the expression of hBD-2 in NHEKs.
source: Neither PSMβ nor the extract resulted in any detectable increase in gene expression, whereas MALP-2 significantly increased the expression of hBD-2, and Poly I:C significantly increased CXCL10 and IL-6 expression (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qPCR shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: Poly I:C significantly increased CXCL10 and IL-6 expression in NHEKs.
source: Neither PSMβ nor the extract resulted in any detectable increase in gene expression, whereas MALP-2 significantly increased the expression of hBD-2, and Poly I:C significantly increased CXCL10 and IL-6 expression (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qPCR shown in Figure 3A–C.

claim: TLR-mediated responses were significantly reduced during co-treatment with S. felis C4 PSMβ or extract.
source: Interestingly, these TLR-mediated responses were significantly reduced during co-treatment with S. felis C4 PSMβ or extract.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qPCR and ELISA assays.

claim: PSMβ2 had a significant effect on suppressing CXCL10 secretion in NHEKs after 24 hr co-treatment.
source: This result was confirmed by ELISA, showing that PSMβ2 had a significant effect on suppressing CXCL10 secretion in NHEKs after 24 hr co-treatment (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from ELISA shown in Figure 3D.

claim: IL-6 and TNFα expression was decreased during co-treatment with S. felis C4 PSMβ2 in human THP-1 macrophage-like cells stimulated with MALP-2 or LPS.
source: To determine if this interaction is specific for epithelial cells, we also stimulated human THP-1 macrophage-like cells with MALP-2, or the TLR4 agonist LPS and found that IL-6 and TNFα expression was decreased during co-treatment with S. felis C4 PSMβ2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qPCR shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The addition of S. felis C4 PSMβ2 to NHEK activated by poly I:C inhibited phosphorylation of TBK1 and IRF3 at 15 min post-stimulation with the peptide.
source: The addition of S. felis C4 PSMβ2 to NHEK activated by poly I:C demonstrated that PSMβ2 inhibited phosphorylation of TBK1 and IRF3 at 15 min post-stimulation with the peptide (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from immunoblot shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Gene ontology (GO) analyses revealed the significant down-regulation of several gene clusters associated with 'immune effector process' and 'type I IFN signaling' at 4 h during co-treatment of PSMβ2 and Poly I:C.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analyses revealed the significant down-regulation of several gene clusters associated with 'immune effector process' and 'type I IFN signaling' at 4 h during co-treatment of PSMβ2 and Poly I:C (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: PSMβ2 treatment alone did not induce an immunological response in NHEKs.
source: A heatmap of selected genes within the 'Immune response' GO term at 4 h post-treatment further highlighted the suppressive effect, and also importantly showed that PSMβ2 treatment alone did not induce an immunological response in NHEKs (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: When NHEKs were treated with PSMβ2 in the absence of an inflammatory stimulus, the downregulation of genes within GO terms such as 'cytokine-mediated signaling' and 'pathogenic E. coli infection' was identified.
source: However, when NHEKs were treated with PSMβ2 in the absence of an inflammatory stimulus, we identified the downregulation of genes within GO terms such as "cytokine-mediated signaling" and "pathogenic E. coli infection" (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting that exposure to PSMβ2 primes cells to dampen potential inflammatory mediators in response to TLR ligands.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Exposure to PSMβ2 primes cells to dampen potential inflammatory mediators in response to TLR ligands.
source: However, when NHEKs were treated with PSMβ2 in the absence of an inflammatory stimulus, we identified the downregulation of genes within GO terms such as "cytokine-mediated signaling" and "pathogenic E. coli infection" (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting that exposure to PSMβ2 primes cells to dampen potential inflammatory mediators in response to TLR ligands.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data from RNA-Seq analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: PSMβ2-upregulated genes were mostly associated with biosynthetic pathways including lipid and amino acid metabolism.
source: This contrasted with PSMβ2-upregulated genes which were mostly associated with biosynthetic pathways including lipid and amino acid metabolism (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: All three synthetic S. felis C4 PSMβ (PSMβ1–3) peptides exhibited antimicrobial activity in inhibiting S. pseudintermedius at a concentration of 50 μg/ml.
source: The antimicrobial activity of all three synthetic S. felis C4 PSMβ (PSMβ1–3) peptides in inhibiting S. pseudintermedius was observed to occur at a concentration of 50 μg/ml and the synthetic EF-HAND domain-containing peptide did not inhibit bacterial growth at concentrations up to 200 μg/ml (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from antimicrobial assays shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The synthetic EF-HAND domain-containing peptide did not inhibit bacterial growth at concentrations up to 200 μg/ml.
source: The antimicrobial activity of all three synthetic S. felis C4 PSMβ (PSMβ1–3) peptides in inhibiting S. pseudintermedius was observed to occur at a concentration of 50 μg/ml and the synthetic EF-HAND domain-containing peptide did not inhibit bacterial growth at concentrations up to 200 μg/ml (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from antimicrobial assays shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The native extract prepared from S. felis supernatant was found to be more potent than the synthetic PSM when added individually or in combination.
source: In contrast, the native extract prepared from S. felis supernatant was found to be more potent than the synthetic PSM when added individually (Figure 3H) or in combination (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from antimicrobial assays shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: A non-N-formylated version of PSMB2 exhibited similar activity to the N-formylated PSMβ2 version.
source: A non-N-formylated version of PSMB2 exhibited similar activity to the N-formylated PSMβ2 version (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from antimicrobial assays shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The disparity in the potency of the synthetic peptides compared to the native extract suggested that another antimicrobial molecule is produced by S. felis C4 that was not detected in the prior analyses.
source: This disparity in the potency of the synthetic peptides compared to the native extract suggested that another antimicrobial molecule is produced by S. felis C4 that was not detected in the prior analyses.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data comparing synthetic peptides and native extract.

claim: Interrogation of the S. felis C4 genome revealed a BCG with similarity to micrococcin P1 from Macrococcus caseolyticus.
source: To investigate this, we conducted further genome analysis using the web server anti-SMASH to identify the potential presence of secondary metabolites encoded from biosynthetic gene clusters (BCG) (Weber et al., 2015). Interrogation of the S. felis C4 genome revealed a BCG with similarity to micrococcin P1 from Macrococcus caseolyticus (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from genome analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Micrococcin P1 is a macrocyclic antibiotic that inhibits ribosome translation in gram-positive bacteria.
source: Micrococcin P1 is a macrocyclic antibiotic that inhibits ribosome translation in gram-positive bacteria (Figure 4B Carnio et al., 2000; Ciufolini and Lefranc, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Synthetic micrococcin P1 eluted as a single major peak at 59% acetonitrile in fractions 27 and 28.
source: To determine if micrococcin P1 could be present within the S. felis C4 extract, we compared the C8 HPLC elution profile of synthetic micrococcin P1 to the native S. felis C4 extract and identified that the synthetic peptide eluted as a single major peak at 59 % acetonitrile in fractions 27 and 28 (Figure 4C).

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cytotoxicity assays.

claim: The smaller PSMs are well characterised toxins that trigger pro-inflammatory responses.
source: These smaller PSMs are well characterised toxins that trigger pro-inflammatory responses (Nakamura et al., 2013; Williams et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The larger PSMβ reportedly does not elicit pro-inflammatory activity in vitro.
source: Whereas the larger PSMβ reportedly does not elicit pro-inflammatory activity in vitro – a finding that was supported by our data, little is known regarding other potential host responses to PSMβ exposure (Cheung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and experimental data.

claim: Little is known regarding other potential host responses to PSMβ exposure.
source: Whereas the larger PSMβ reportedly does not elicit pro-inflammatory activity in vitro – a finding that was supported by our data, little is known regarding other potential host responses to PSMβ exposure (Cheung et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: When both NHEKs and THP-1 macrophages were treated with S. felis PSMs or extract in the presence of TLR agonists, cytokine induction was reduced but most evidently by PSMβ2.
source: Indeed, when both NHEKs and THP-1 macrophages were treated with S. felis PSMs or extract in the presence of TLR agonists, cytokine induction was reduced but most evidently by PSMβ2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from qPCR and ELISA assays.

claim: RNA-Seq analysis of NHEKs revealed global suppression of inflammatory pathways typically activated by TLR3, in the presence of PSMβ2.
source: RNA-Seq analysis of NHEKs revealed global suppression of inflammatory pathways typically activated by TLR3, in the presence of PSMβ2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: S. felis C4 has low cytotoxicity and broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity and anti-inflammatory activity and is therefore an attractive biotherapeutic candidate for treatment of skin disease.
source: Taken together, here we report that S. felis C4 has low cytotoxicity and broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity and anti-inflammatory activity and is therefore an attractive biotherapeutic candidate for treatment of skin disease.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data and speculation about potential applications.
